summary: Essex County, NY lookout on Mount Adams; the present 1917 steel tower stands after a 2010-era volunteer restoration, on private land with current public access unclear.

facts.design: 1917 Aermotor LS-40 steel tower with a 7-by-7-foot metal cab (register: 47 ft; Wikipedia: 56-ft steel frame); 1922 observer's cabin, the register's only surviving Model 1922 in New York State

staffing.status: state-staffed until the mid 1970s; volunteers now help maintain the trail and tower

access.note: NYSDEC describes the tower as on private property within the High Peaks Wilderness; the register says the Open Space Institute administers it; ADK says it had been closed to the public as a safety hazard before its restoration. Current public access is not confirmed.

visit.trail_note: hiking trail to the summit; ADK says the last half mile gains 1,000 feet in just a half mile

facts.agency: Open Space Institute of New York

events.note: first tower on the site was a wooden structure built at the request of the Tahawus Club
state erected the present steel Aermotor LS-40 tower
ground house and observer's cabin; the register calls the cabin a Model 1922
improvements made to the ground house
National Historic Lookout Register registration date February 12, 2004
added to the National Register of Historic Places April 12, 2006
Friends of Mt Adams began restoration work on the observer's cabin in September 2007
ADK Highpeaks Foundation says that by 2010 the tower had fallen into disrepair and was closed to the public as a safety hazard
ADK Highpeaks Foundation was approached in 2010 about restoring the tower; it describes about three years of volunteer restoration work
spring 2011 flooding destroyed the steel cable bridge over the Hudson River, forcing volunteers to ford the river

corrections.proposed: 1912 first tower was a wooden structure; present steel tower erected 1917
corrections.why: The register's 'Built 1912' field refers to the first wooden tower. The present 47-foot steel Aermotor tower was erected by the state in 1917, per the register's description and ADK.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The register and ADK describe a 47-foot Aermotor LS-40 tower. Wikipedia describes a 56-foot-tall steel frame tower (17 m). The story reports both figures and does not choose one.

The NYSDEC says the tower sits on private property within the High Peaks Wilderness. The register says the Open Space Institute administers it. The two are not necessarily in conflict, but the sources do not state who owns the land or whether the public may climb.

notes_for_editor: The brief's 1912 'built' event refers to the first wooden tower; the present steel tower dates from 1917. The height conflict (47 ft in NHLR and ADK vs 56 ft in Wikipedia) is unresolved. Current public access is not confirmed: NYSDEC calls the land private and the tower restored, the register says OSI administers it, and ADK describes closure before its volunteer restoration. The access level is set to restricted for that reason and should be re-checked with OSI or NYSDEC. The 2010 'closed' event year is the year of ADK's account, not the closure date. The LA Times 2004 article on the wilderness debate and an andyarthur.org page were not readable (403), so they are not cited. The staffed_last year is not an event because the register says only 'the mid 1970s'. Wikipedia's retrieval date is October 29, 2025 per its reference list, not the accessed date.
